Tropical Storm Choi-wan continues to move away from Anatahan and is
inching closer to Alamagan, pivoting slowly to the north-northeast 
through Saturday. During this time, the wind field will continue to 
expand, exposing Tinian and Saipan in Tropical Storm conditions a
little longer, now through Saturday. As such, a Tropical Storm
Warning remains in effect for Tinian and Saipan. While showers have 
tapered a little due to a dry slot overhead, rainbands that pummeled
Guam and Rota earlier this morning are now being pulled toward 
Tinian and Saipan, with more intense showers and thunderstorms 
expected tonight. After a lull in showers and thunderstorms expires 
soon, periods of rain, widespread heavy showers and some 
thunderstorms are expected to return and continue to pummel Tinian 
and Saipan tonight, to then taper down thereafter as Choi-wan moves 
away. Similar at Guam and Rota, albeit only patchy showers and some 
thunderstorms expected overnight brought by very fresh to strong 
southwesterlies. A drier monsoon pattern will return early next week,
with low-end scattered showers and a thunderstorm or two expected to
develop through next Friday. For more information, please refer to
the local statement issued by the National Weather Service under WMO
header WTPQ82 PGUM.

Marine...
Hazardous seas of 15 to 20 feet and dangerous surf of 10 to 14 feet
along south and west facing reefs will persist through Saturday, 
then begin to gradually diminish as Tropical Storm Choi-wan (26W) 
moves away from the northern CNMI and brings elevated southwest 
monsoon swell to the Marianas. In addition to a secondary northerly 
swell and massive localized wind waves, hazardous seas, gale-force 
winds and dangerous surf are expected through the weekend. There will
be a high risk of rip currents along north, west and south facing 
reefs of Guam and Rota. The north facing reefs could diminish to 
moderate along north facing reefs while continuing to be high along 
south and west facing reefs through at least Sunday night.

Hydrology...
Multiple flood advisories were issued across the Marianas today, with
a Flash Flood Warning issued for the southern portions of Guam where
the heaviest cells made their way across this morning. Preliminary
satellite-based rain estimates indicate a total of 3 to 5 inches of
rain may have fallen across the Marianas, while various sensors
across Guam have measured between 2 and 3 inches of rain during this
rain event so far, with a peak observed at American Memorial Park, 
Saipan at just under 4 inches so far. After Choi-wan's passage this 
weekend, a trailing monsoon inflow band will maintain wet conditions 
into early next week, resulting in 4 to 6 inches of rain for Guam and
Rota, and 5 to 8 inches for Tinian and Saipan during the Watch 
period.

Tropical Systems...
At 1 PM ChST, the center of Tropical Storm Choi-wan (26W) was located
near latitude 17.2N and longitude 144.7E. This was about 260 miles 
north of Guam. Choi-wan is moving west-northwest at 5 mph, slowing 
down before pivoting toward the north-northeast with little change in
forward speed through Saturday as it moves up the Far Northern 
Marianas. Maximum sustained winds have increased to 65 mph. Choi-wan 
is forecast to intensify through tonight, possibly becoming a typhoon
later today. Tropical storm force winds continue to extend outward 
from the center up to 125 miles, however, the wind field is expected 
to expand farther south over the next few hours as Choi-wan continues
to indulge in very favorable shear conditions over the northern 
CNMI. At this time, a Tropical Storm Warning remains in effect for 
Saipan, Tinian and their adjacent coastal waters, as well as Alamagan,
Pagan, and Agrihan. In addition, a Typhoon Watch remains in effect 
for Alamagan, Pagan, and Agrihan.

Further south and east, Invest 94W was dubbed by JTWC (the Joint
typhoon Warning Center) earlier this morning, as a low-level 
circulation has become somewhat better organized north of Kwajalein. 
This feature looks to meander in the area for a few days (through 
Sunday or Monday), possibly allowing another weak circulation 
northeast of Majuro to merge with it. Then, all of the ensembles and 
AI-driven models lift this system off to the north and then northwest
as it organizes for the middle to end of next week. At this point, 
the main impacts from 94W will be potentially prolonging and 
enhancing a westerly swell across a goof portion of the FSM and RMI, 
potentially leading to some minor inundation concerns developing 
over the weekend. Also, the GFS has hinted at some convective gusts 
near 30 mph, with todays scatterometer pass showing similar values 
south and southeast of Majuro. With that said, the models show this 
burst of winds dampening out over the next 24 to 36 hours, but this 
is something we'll keep an eye on.
